title: The Myth of the Evidence-Based Curriculum sed-on-student-learning-data/
author: Morgan S. Polikoff and Jake Rowley
summary: Morgan Polikoff and Jake Rowley argue that calls to choose curriculum materials based on student learning data are currently impractical. States are interested in effective curricula and the research community in rigorous evaluation, but the two have not combined, largely because states never tracked which curricula schools adopt and the ESSA evidence tiers fit core materials poorly. The tiers allow a Tier 1 label from an experiment of just 350 students across two sites and a minimum of twelve weeks, too small and short for curriculum effects, and a review of 36 public studies found few that named a comparison curriculum. They say publishers are not the villains: they face unrealistic timelines, recruitment difficulties, validity and implementation problems, the replication crisis and cost barriers. Their recommendations are to stop demanding strong causal evidence before every adoption, to have states or philanthropy fund independent evaluation infrastructure, and to improve guidelines with longer time horizons and larger samples.
points: States have failed to collect curriculum adoption data, leaving independent researchers unable to study what works.
The ESSA evidence tiers privilege small, short experiments, which is a poor match for evaluating a full year of core curriculum.
Most published studies compare against unspecified business-as-usual curricula, so they cannot tell districts which product is better.
Publishers face real obstacles to rigorous evaluation, including timelines, recruiting schools for random assignment and the expense of development.
Districts should treat curriculum choice as a judgement informed by evidence rather than a clinical-trial decision, with states funding independent evaluation.
quotes: Curriculum materials are having a policy moment. After more than a quarter-century of standards-based reform, policymakers are recognizing that these reforms will likely not improve student learning without attention to the quality of the materials in teachers’ hands.

While it’s tempting to blame the curriculum companies and technology providers, the problem is more nuanced: States have failed to track which curricula schools are adopting, leaving independent researchers without the data needed to study what works.

Sixteen used statistical methods that failed to take into account that students experiencing the curriculum were grouped within classrooms or schools. Others exhibited clear evidence of selection bias or puzzling exclusions of data.

Neither have other states taken the necessary steps to generate evidence on curriculum effects that could inform district decisions. Yes, some states have started collecting data on curriculum adoptions and making it available, but they haven’t advanced to using those data for evaluations.

But how can they evaluate their materials if they can’t sell them to schools and districts in order to conduct an evaluation? Often curriculum adoption decisions come shortly after standards revisions, but companies need time to adapt their materials to new standards.
Measuring student outcomes. Evaluation of curriculum materials requires some measure of student outcomes, usually the state test.
The adoption of open-science principles and more careful design would help address these issues, but this would again require independent leadership and a more centralized structure.
These methods can include quasi-experimental investigations and simpler designs that compare value added to student achievement across schools adopting different curriculum materials.
